submission.natural_language_explanation: Fires on the descriptive/encyclopedic nominal lexicon that locates things in a world: common nouns naming places, land and its features, settlements, structures, collectives, populations and periods (Europe, pasture, ground, landscape, valley, villages, towns, schools, buildings, region, population, century, system) and the generalising adjectives that modify them (general, natural, modern, ancient, traditional), while staying near zero on function words, basic high-frequency verbs (make, find, include), body-part nouns (head, skin, blood) and household-object nouns (spoon, plate, carpet). The class is graded rather than categorical ('Europe' 0.77 and 'pasture' 0.76 vs 'France' 0.26 and 'design' -0.11 in a fixed frame), and the unit reacts to the token already read rather than preparing a specific next token (zero-ablation KL 1.4e-4, Jacobian kurtosis 2.9, lens agreement 0%), with the very strongest single activations being word-internal fragments of long descriptive words ('nt' in Florentia, 'cent' in reconcentrated) as an acknowledged leftover.

adversarial_test_results.detail: Body-part nouns (head, skin, blood) in a household accident; the hypothesis explicitly predicts near-zero on body-part nouns.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She set a spoon beside every plate, then beat the crumbs out of the carpet with the flat of her hand.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Household-object nouns (spoon, plate, carpet) with none of the claimed place/land lexicon; the hypothesis excludes this class.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: You can make the sauce ahead of time, find a clean jar in the cupboard, and include a pinch of salt at the end.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: It is what it is, and if that is how they want it done, then so be it.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A pure function-word sentence whose 'so' is the standalone discourse marker (not the word-initial fragment seen in the soybean/sonal examples); the hypothesis predicts function words are near zero.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Their cover band played Europe's biggest hit at the wedding reception, and the older guests sang every word.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed token 'Europe' names a band here rather than a place; the hypothesis's class is place-naming nouns, so it predicts this sense is outside the class even though the token string matches.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She ground the beans by hand, poured the coffee into a chipped mug, and carried it out to the porch.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed token 'ground' is used as a cooking verb in a kitchen scene, a sense the land-feature class excludes.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The stamp cost a single cent in 1890, and a used copy now sells for thousands at auction.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The 'cent' token (the same token that peaks word-internally in 'reconcentrated') appears as a currency unit in a price sentence with no place, land or period noun, which the hypothesis's class does not cover.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The design of the poster was approved after two rounds of revisions, and printing began on Friday.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Uses 'design', which the hypothesis itself grades at -0.11 against the class, as an abstract design-register noun with no place or land content.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Investors hedged their positions before the earnings call, and the stock barely moved by the close.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The 'hed' token appears word-internally exactly as in the watershed example, but inside a finance verb with none of the claimed lexicon; the hypothesis scopes its fragment leftover to long descriptive words, so it predicts near zero here.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: It is only natural to feel nervous before a performance, and the instructor said as much.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed adjective 'natural' appears as a predicate about an emotion rather than as a generalising modifier of a place or land noun, the role the hypothesis claims for it.

adversarial_test_results.detail: History prose with period, settlement, population, generalising adjective and settlement nouns (century, town, population, general), a novel genre for the claimed class.

Every spring the survey crew returned to the northern tract, where the soil stayed wet well into June and the access track had to be rebuilt after the thaw. The work was slow and mostly unglamorous: staking plots, noting where the drainage failed, arguing over which boundary marker the previous contractor had moved. By the second season the maps had grown detailed enough to be worth copying, and the county office began asking for duplicates. The crew chief, who had spent a decade on similar jobs in other parts of the country, insisted that the early notes be kept with the later ones, because the later measurements meant little without them. She dated the corner of every page and numbered the pages twice, in case the first numbering came undone in the rain. New assistants found her exacting and were usually right to. The equipment shed leaked, the generator was unreliable, and the coffee was terrible, but nobody quit.

The findings, when they finally went to the printer, were modest. Runoff was faster on the cleared slopes than on the wooded ones, and the difference held through two dry summers and one very wet one. The crew logged each reading twice and photographed every site from the same three angles on every visit, which took longer than anyone had budgeted for. Nothing in the numbers surprised the people who had walked the land for years. The surprise, if there was one, was how much of each season's budget went on replacing instruments that had been dropped, lost in gullies, or had simply stopped working.

By the end of the programme the county had a set of documents it could actually use: contour lines, soil types, drainage channels, and notes on every damaged culvert between the ridge and the highway. Some of it would be obsolete within a decade, but it was a better record than anything that had existed before. The final report closed with a short chapter on what had changed since the first survey, and there the authors allowed themselves a little colour: the valley below the ridge had lost three farmsteads, gained a small reservoir, and seen the villages along the river double in size as commuters moved out from the city. The landscape, they wrote, was no longer a farming one; it was becoming something else, and nobody could yet say what the next century would make of it.
